turns.prompt_text: We've got this box of bee comb frames and there's a good amount of nectar in them There's also some picnic beetles within them We are wondering if picnic beetles will eat the pollen
turns.response_html:
Yes, picnic beetles will absolutely eat the pollen.

Picnic beetles (broadly known as sap beetles) are scavengers naturally drawn to sweet, fermenting, and protein-rich food sources. Since your bee comb frames contain both nectar (sugar) and pollen (protein), they offer a perfect meal for these insects.

The Small Hive Beetle Risk

Because you are dealing with bee comb, there is a critical distinction to make. Small Hive Beetles (SHB) belong to the exact same insect family (Nitidulidae) as regular picnic beetles and look almost identical. While a standard picnic beetle is mostly just a nuisance, the Small Hive Beetle is a highly destructive pest for a honeybee colony.

If the insects in your frames are actually Small Hive Beetles, they pose a severe threat:

  • Comb Destruction: Adult beetles lay eggs in the crevices of the comb. The hatching larvae tunnel through the wax, aggressively consuming pollen, nectar, and bee brood.
  • Fermentation and Slime: As the larvae feed, they defecate inside the cells. This introduces a yeast that causes the nectar to ferment and bubble, turning the frame into a ruined, slimy mess that smells strongly of rotting oranges. Bees will completely reject "slimed" comb and may even abandon the hive if the infestation is severe.

How to Protect the Frames

If this box of frames is currently sitting out of a hive, the safest move is to freeze the frames for at least 48 hours. Freezing kills any adult beetles, hidden eggs, or larvae without damaging the wax structure, nectar, or pollen. Once thawed, the frames are safe to put into a hive or store away.

turns.prompt_text: We have another a number of wax comb frames with pollen in them and we can't use them because the bees won't use the pollen so we want to get the pollen out So we were thinking that putting a bunch of these beetles onto it will help eat it away
turns.response_html:
While the beetles would certainly eat the pollen, intentionally introducing them to your frames is a recipe for disaster. Using beetles as a cleanup crew will destroy the very wax comb you are trying to save and put your active colonies at massive risk.

Here is exactly why this method backfires, and how you should actually get the pollen out.

Why the "Beetle Method" Will Ruin Your Frames

  • Comb Destruction: Beetles don't just gently eat the pollen. The adults will lay eggs, and the resulting larvae will aggressively tunnel through the wax cells to get to the food, chewing up the structure of the comb.
  • The "Slime" Factor: As beetle larvae feed, they defecate everywhere. This introduces a specific yeast that ferments remaining nectar and pollen residues, turning the entire frame into a putrid, bubbling, slimy mess. Once a frame is slimed, the wax is effectively ruined, and bees will refuse to use it.
  • Creating a Pest Explosion: By giving beetles an unprotected food source, you are essentially building a breeding ground. This will create a massive local population of beetles that will inevitably seek out and invade your active, healthy hives.

How to Safely Remove Hardened Pollen

If the bees are ignoring the pollen (often because it has dried out and hardened into "pollen bricks"), you can clean the frames while preserving the valuable drawn wax.

1. The Soak and Spray Method (Best for Preserving Comb) This is the most reliable way to save the drawn comb for future use.

  • Soak: Submerge the frames completely in a tub of clean, room-temperature water for 24 to 48 hours. This rehydrates and softens the rock-hard pollen.
  • Spray: Take the frames out and use a garden hose with a moderate spray nozzle. Blast the water directly into the cells. The softened pollen will blow right out.
  • Dry: Shake out the excess water and let the frames dry completely in a well-ventilated, sunlit area (to prevent wax moths and mold) before putting them in storage or back in a hive.

2. The Scraping Method (Best for Concentrated Areas) If the pollen is localized to just a few patches on the frame, take your hive tool and scrape that specific section of comb all the way down to the plastic or wax foundation. The bees will readily rebuild the wax in that small area when you place the frame back into a strong hive during a nectar flow.

3. Melt and Restart (For Fully Bound Frames) If a frame is completely "pollen bound" edge-to-edge and washing it out is too tedious, the best course of action is to cut the comb out entirely. You can melt the comb down to salvage the beeswax and put fresh foundation in the frame to let the bees start over.
